opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it a bit differently: SGLang has always been an open-source project with its own community, and that hasn't changed. What drew me to xAI was the chance to work on inference at a scale where every efficiency improvement really matters.

When you build a serving system in academia, you're guessing at real production problems. You benchmark on public models and synthetic workloads, and you hope the optimizations hold up. At a company training and serving frontier models, you see the actual bottlenecks: long-context requests, huge batch sizes, mixed workloads, hardware pushed to its limits. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable. Problems show up faster, and they're harder and more interesting.

There's also the culture. The team moves very fast and is very engineering-driven. If something can be made faster, people want it done this week, not next quarter. Systems work fits that mindset well. You can try an idea in the morning, measure it, and know by the evening whether it was worth it.

For me, the most important thing is that this work flows back into the open-source side. Many techniques we refine under real load, like better scheduling, caching, and kernel optimizations, end up benefiting everyone who uses SGLang. That combination was what I was looking for: a hard production environment that pushes the system forward, and a community that makes the improvements widely available.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the decision came down to one thing: where was the gap between what SGLang could do and what it needed to do the largest, and where would closing that gap matter most.

SGLang started as an academic project at Berkeley. The early question was simple: LLM programs are getting complicated, with multi-turn calls, structured outputs, tool use, and a lot of shared prefixes, so can we build a runtime that treats inference as a program rather than a sequence of isolated requests? That gave us things like RadixAttention for prefix caching and the constrained decoding work. It worked well in a research setting, and it got real adoption in open source.

But there's a ceiling you hit in academia. You can show that an idea is good on eight GPUs. You cannot easily show it is good on tens of thousands, with real traffic, real latency budgets, and real cost pressure. And frankly, a lot of the hardest problems in serving only appear at that scale. Load balancing across a disaggregated prefill and decode fleet, cache placement, how you handle very long contexts, how you keep utilization high when request patterns shift by the hour. You don't discover those problems by reading papers. You discover them because something is on fire at two in the morning.

xAI had three things I cared about. First, the scale was real and immediate. Grok was serving a lot of users, and the team was building out compute aggressively, so any improvement in the serving stack translated directly into capacity and cost. That kind of feedback loop is a researcher's dream. Second, the team was small enough and moving fast enough that infrastructure decisions could actually be made. At a larger company you often spend a year arguing about which framework to standardize on. Here, if the engine was better, it got used. Third, and this mattered to me personally, there was genuine openness to keeping SGLang open source. I didn't want the project to become a proprietary fork that the community lost. The understanding was that the hard problems we solved in production would flow back into the public project, and that's what has happened.

I'd also say there's a cultural fit. The engineering culture at xAI is very bottom-up and very hands-on. People who write the kernels are the same people who get paged. For a systems person, that's where you want to be, because the only way to really understand inference is to own it end to end.

So the short version is: SGLang needed a place where it would be stress-tested by a frontier model at frontier scale, and I needed a place where that work would stay open. xAI was the intersection of those two.
